deep.reconstruction:
Overview. The page derives the linear (connection) relations between branches of Riemann P-functions. It does so from a projectively symmetric four-point Euler integral and Cauchy's theorem. The method is the one used in Riemann's 1857 paper on Gauss's series. The previous page treated a degenerate (logarithmic) case of such relations and remarked that one reaches the goal more easily by starting from series. This page instead starts from integrals.

(1) Setup. Let Z = (z-a)^alpha (z-b)^beta (z-c)^gamma (z-d)^delta with real a<b<c<d. Riemann integrates Z along the real axis from -R to R and closes the path with a large half-circle from +R back to -R in the lower half-plane, so arg runs from 0 to -pi. Implicitly the branch points are also passed on the lower side.
- Each factor (z-a)^alpha is taken real for z>a. Continued through the lower half-plane, for z<a it equals e^{-alpha pi i}(a-z)^alpha.
- Write (Z) for the modulus (real positive value) of Z on each interval.
- The integral over the closed path is 0:
  e^{-pi(alpha+beta+gamma+delta)i} int_{-inf}^a (Z)dz + e^{-pi(beta+gamma+delta)i} int_a^b (Z)dz + e^{-pi(gamma+delta)i} int_b^c (Z)dz + e^{-pi delta i} int_c^d (Z)dz + int_d^inf (Z)dz = 0.

(2) Choice of exponents. Riemann sets e^{-pi(alpha+beta+gamma+delta)i} = 1. In context this means alpha+beta+gamma+delta = -2 (my reading).
- Then Z dz is regular at infinity, so the half-circle contributes nothing (Z ~ z^{-2}).
- The integral is projectively invariant.
- The pieces from -inf to a and from d to inf merge into one integral (d,a) through infinity.
- With (a,b) = int_a^b (Z)dz etc., and using beta+gamma+delta = -2-alpha etc., the relation becomes:
  (d,a) + e^{i pi alpha}(a,b) + e^{i pi(alpha+beta)}(b,c) + e^{i pi(alpha+beta+gamma)}(c,d) = 0.
- Multiply by e^{i k pi} and take imaginary parts:
  (a,b) sin(k+alpha)pi + (b,c) sin(k+alpha+beta)pi + (c,d) sin(k+alpha+beta+gamma)pi + (d,a) sin(k pi) = 0 for all k.
- This amounts to two independent real relations.

(3) Reduction to the cross-ratio. Set x = (a-b)(c-d)/((a-c)(b-d)). Then 1-x = (a-d)(b-c)/((a-c)(b-d)), and 0<x<1 for a<b<c<d.
- Each of the four integrals, up to elementary factors (powers of x, 1-x and of the differences, which he does not write out), is a branch of a P-function. Its exponent differences are:
  lambda = alpha+beta+1 at x=0, mu = alpha+gamma+1 at x=inf, nu = alpha+delta+1 at x=1.
- Because the exponents sum to -2, gamma+delta+1 = -lambda and beta+gamma+1 = -nu. This is his remark P(alpha+beta+1, alpha+gamma+1, alpha+delta+1) = P(gamma+delta+1, gamma+alpha+1, gamma+beta+1), i.e. (lambda,mu,nu) vs (-lambda,mu,-nu).
- The +1/6 in the exponents: my interpretation is the symmetric normalisation of P-exponents, 1/6 ± lambda/2 etc. Their sum is 1, as in Riemann 1857.
- Branch identification:
  - (a,b) is the branch at 0 with exponent lambda, i.e. P(lambda,mu,nu,x).
  - (c,d) is the branch at 0 with -lambda, i.e. P(-lambda,-mu,nu,x).
  - (d,a) is the branch at 1 with nu, i.e. P(nu,mu,lambda,1-x).
  - (b,c) is the branch at 1 with -nu, i.e. P(-nu,-mu,lambda,1-x).

(4) First specialisation, k=0 (kills (d,a)). Using sin(alpha+beta+gamma)pi = sin(-2-delta)pi = -sin(delta pi):
  (b,c) sin(alpha+beta)pi = -sin(alpha pi)(a,b) + sin(delta pi)(c,d).

(5) Second specialisation, k = -(alpha+beta) (kills (b,c)). Using sin(-(alpha+beta))pi = sin(gamma+delta)pi:
  (d,a) sin(gamma+delta)pi = sin(beta pi)(a,b) - sin(gamma pi)(c,d).
He rewrites both in branch notation.

(6) Rewriting in lambda, mu, nu. The substitutions are:
- alpha = (lambda+mu+nu-1)/2, beta = (lambda-mu-nu-1)/2, gamma = (mu-lambda-nu-1)/2, delta = (nu-lambda-mu-1)/2.
- sin(gamma+delta)pi = sin(lambda pi), sin(beta pi) = -cos((lambda-mu-nu)pi/2), sin(gamma pi) = -cos((mu-lambda-nu)pi/2).
Relation (5) becomes
  P(nu,mu,lambda,1-x) sin(lambda pi) = -P(lambda,mu,nu,x) cos((lambda-mu-nu)pi/2) + P(-lambda,-mu,nu,x) cos((-lambda+mu-nu)pi/2).
This is exactly as written on the page.

Relation (4) gives, with sin(alpha+beta)pi = -sin(lambda pi), sin(alpha pi) = -cos((lambda+mu+nu)pi/2), sin(delta pi) = -cos((lambda+mu-nu)pi/2):
  P(-nu,-mu,lambda,1-x) sin(lambda pi) = -P(lambda,mu,nu,x) cos((lambda+mu+nu)pi/2) + P(-lambda,-mu,nu,x) cos((lambda+mu-nu)pi/2).

(7) Closing remark. Riemann notes that the remaining equations follow by reversing the signs of mu and nu. Indeed (6b) is (6a) with mu -> -mu, nu -> -nu, given that the branch labels depend only on the sign of the exponent at the relevant point.

Summary. The page is a draft of the sine-coefficient connection formulas between the x=0 and x=1 bases of a P-function. They are obtained from a projectively symmetric four-point integral by deforming the integration path into the lower half-plane.
errors: In the last formula the second coefficient reads cos((-lambda+mu+nu)pi/2) in the transcription, possibly cut off in the image. Direct derivation from (b,c) sin(alpha+beta)pi = -sin(alpha pi)(a,b) + sin(delta pi)(c,d), and also Riemann's own rule (mu,nu -> -mu,-nu applied to the previous line), gives cos((lambda+mu-nu)pi/2), equivalently cos((-lambda-mu+nu)pi/2). This is likely a slip, or a misreading of a partly cut-off expression.

The elementary prefactors attached to the four integrals are incomplete and partly inconsistent as written. The exponents carry a +1/6 whose sign relative to the normalisation 1/6 ± lambda/2 is unclear. The factor x^{(alpha+beta+1)/2} in the first rewritten relation lacks the 1/6. The x^{delta+gamma+1} lacks the /2. The factors in the differences a-b etc. that make the integrals functions of x alone are omitted. These are working notes, not a final normalisation.

The vanishing of the half-circle contribution and the merging of int_{-inf}^a with int_d^inf require alpha+beta+gamma+delta = -2. This is only indicated by 'e^{-pi(alpha+beta+gamma+delta)i} = 1', which as written would allow any even integer. Convergence at the endpoints, Re(alpha),...,Re(delta) > -1, is implicit.
Several cancelled false starts on the page are harmless.

results.what: Linear relation among the four interval integrals (a,b),(b,c),(c,d),(d,a) of (z-a)^alpha (z-b)^beta (z-c)^gamma (z-d)^delta with exponent sum -2. It is obtained by Cauchy's theorem on a lower half-plane contour: sum of (interval) * sin(k + partial exponent sum)pi = 0.
results.modern_name: Contour-deformation (monodromy) relations for Euler/Pochhammer-type integrals; twisted cycle relations
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1857 (Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe darstellbaren Functionen) for the hypergeometric case; later Pochhammer (1890), Klein's lectures (1894)

results.what: Projectively symmetric four-point form of the Euler integral (exponent sum -2), reduced to a function of the cross-ratio x=(a-b)(c-d)/((a-c)(b-d)). The four interval integrals are identified with the branches P(±lambda,...) at 0 and at 1, with lambda=alpha+beta+1, mu=alpha+gamma+1, nu=alpha+delta+1.
results.modern_name: Projectively invariant Euler integral representation of Riemann's P-function
results.usually_credited_to: Commonly presented in Klein's 'Vorlesungen über die hypergeometrische Funktion' (1894); the underlying idea is Riemann's

results.what: Connection formulas between the x=0 and x=1 branches of P with sine/cosine coefficients: P(nu,mu,lambda,1-x) sin(lambda pi) = -P(lambda,mu,nu,x) cos((lambda-mu-nu)pi/2) + P(-lambda,-mu,nu,x) cos((-lambda+mu-nu)pi/2), and its sign-flipped companion.
results.modern_name: Connection (Kummer-type) relations for the hypergeometric/P-function in Riemann's symmetric normalisation
results.usually_credited_to: Kummer (1836) in Gamma-function form; Riemann (1857) in normalised sine form

deep.surprise_reason: The contour method and the sine-normalised connection relations are exactly what Riemann published in 1857. Using a symmetric four-point integral with exponent sum -2 and the cross-ratio is an elegant variant usually associated with Klein's later lectures, but it is a natural draft of Riemann's own approach, so it is only mildly notable.

checkable.asserts: 1-x for the cross-ratio x equals (a-d)(b-c)/((a-c)(b-d)), so 0<x<1 when a<b<c<d

checkable.asserts: All zero: the trigonometric conversions that turn the sine relations into Riemann's cos((±lambda±mu±nu)/2)pi form. They show the last coefficient should be cos((lambda+mu-nu)pi/2).

transcription_corrections: '0<1' is presumably '0<x<1' (the range of the cross-ratio).

The line beginning 'e^{-pi(alpha+beta+gamma+delta)i}=1 |' continues as '(d,a) + e^{-pi(beta+gamma+delta)i}(a,b) + e^{-pi(gamma+delta)i}(b,c) + e^{-pi delta i}(c,d) = 0'. The partial '+e^{-pi}' is the start of the (b,c) term, and '+(d,a)' is written above the line.
In 'Dieser [?] von -R bis +R ...' the sense is: the path runs from -R to +R through real values and returns from +R to -R along the half-circle, on which the argument passes from 0 to -pi.
'(Z)' is defined (cancelled text) as the modulus ('Mod.') of Z, i.e. the real positive value on each interval.
The final coefficient in the last formula may read cos((-lambda-mu+nu)/2)pi, or is cut off at the page edge. Mathematically it should equal cos((lambda+mu-nu)/2)pi.
The final sentence probably ends 'das entgegengesetzte Zeichen gibt' ('gives mu and nu the opposite sign').
